# Devatā Saṁyutta (SN 1)

**ID:** SN 1  
**Section:** Saṁyuttanikāya (sn)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Devatā Saṁyutta  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0301m.mul0.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0301m.mul0.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Devatā Saṁyutta* (or *Devatāsaṁyutta*, "Linked Discourses With Deities") is the opening section of the *Saṁyuttanikāya*. The collection depicts the Buddha in dialogue with various deities (*devatā*s), typically opening as an effulgent deity visits the Buddha at night in the monastery at Sāvatthī. The deities in this collection are exclusively male, and while female deities appear elsewhere in Buddhist literature, there is no corresponding *Devīsamyutta* [Williams, Critical Concepts; Skilling, Female Roles]. The visiting devatā poses a question, riddle, challenge, praise, or reflection, which the Buddha answers by elevating the exchange to an ethical or spiritual plane [Norman 1983]. Editorial framing across the vaggas varies systematically: the opening discourse provides a narrative introduction describing the setting and the deity's arrival, but subsequent suttas abbreviate or drop the narrative framework entirely, preserving only the verse exchanges [Norman 1983]. The verses are predominantly ethical in orientation, often consisting of riddles, question-and-answer pairs, or wordplays [Norman 1983].

While described in traditional thematic overviews as containing 81 discourses, the collection contains 71 individual suttas in the standard digital arrangement, all of which possess known early parallels. Extensive counterparts are preserved in the two Chinese translations of the *Saṁyuktāgama*: the *Bieyi za ahan jing* (T 100, containing 63 parallels) and the main *Saṁyuktāgama* (T 99, containing 59 parallels), with additional parallels found in Sanskrit fragments (such as SHT Sutta 41 to SN 1.27) and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitopadeśa* (T 1509).
